design_detail: Prospective general-population birth cohort (Christchurch Health and Development Study; 1,265 children born in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 1977), with self-reported methamphetamine (or amphetamine) use and violence over four periods (ages 18–21, 21–25, 25–30, 30–35) reported at interviews at 21, 25, 30 and 35. Population-averaged logistic GEE models relate any use in a period to violence perpetration, violence victimisation and intimate-partner violence perpetration and victimisation in the same period, unadjusted, adjusted for childhood and adolescent confounders (Model 1) and additionally for time-varying covariates (Model 2). A separate logistic regression relates the heaviest frequency of use at ages 18–35 to violence at any time in those years (dose-response, adjusted for fixed confounders only). Ecstasy use is analysed the same way as a comparison, and population attributable fractions are estimated.
can_establish: Whether, in an unselected birth cohort, periods with self-reported methamphetamine use go with more self-reported violence perpetration and victimisation in the same period after adjustment for a wide set of prospectively measured childhood and adolescent factors and for concurrent mental-health, alcohol and cannabis disorders.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine use preceded or caused the violence (use and violence are reported for the same three-to-five-year periods, as the authors state), that other illicit drug use or involvement in drug markets does not explain the association (not adjusted for), or anything about methamphetamine as distinct from amphetamine (both are in the exposure question).

sample.recruitment: Birth cohort: 1,265 children (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch in 1977, studied at birth, 4 months, yearly to 16 and at 18, 21, 25, 30 and 35 (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All cohort members interviewed at any of the last four waves; no exclusions are described.
sample.demographics: Born 1977; equal numbers of boys and girls at birth; ethnicity (Māori or Pacific against European or other) is a covariate, but its distribution is not given in the article (details in an online supplement, not read).
sample.attrition: Interviewed: 1,025 at 21, 1,003 at 25, 987 at 30 and 962 at 35, 76–81% of the original cohort (p. 2); 1,044 people contribute to the dose-response analysis (Table 3). How missing waves were handled, and whether people lost to follow-up differed in drug use or violence, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Unselected general-population cohort; losses of about a fifth by age 35 could be selective, because people who use drugs often and are involved in violence are often harder to retain.

exposure.measurement: At each interview, self-reported use of "methamphetamine, speed, P, ice, etc" since the last interview, coded as any or no use in each period; for the dose-response analysis, the highest frequency reported in any period (never; once or twice only; up to about monthly; at least weekly) (pp. 2–3). No biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency categories only; any use in the periods was 5.5% (18–21), 22.4% (21–25), 14.4% (25–30) and 7.8% (30–35); over ages 18–35, 71.9% never used, 11.9% used once or twice only, 11.3% up to about monthly and 4.9% at least weekly in at least one period (p. 3). Amount and route not measured.
exposure.polysubstance: Model 2 adjusts for alcohol and cannabis use disorders in each period (Table 2 note); other illicit drug use (opioids, cocaine, ecstasy) is not adjusted for. Ecstasy, used by 38.5% of the cohort, is analysed separately and shows no statistically significant adjusted association with violence, which the authors describe as inconclusive evidence (p. 3; p. 5; results in a supplement, not read).

comparison.controls: Within the cohort: periods (or, for the dose-response analysis, people) without methamphetamine use.
comparison.matching: No matching. Model 1 adjusts for parental age, family socioeconomic status at birth, family living standards, family instability, parental intimate-partner violence, parental alcohol problems, criminality and illicit drug use, quality of parenting, childhood sexual and physical abuse, sex, ethnicity, child IQ, school performance, childhood conduct and attention problems, self-esteem, novelty seeking, adolescent conduct disorder, depression, anxiety, smoking and delinquent or substance-using peers; Model 2 adds depression, anxiety disorder, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms in each period (Table 2 notes).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Childhood and adolescent factors were measured prospectively, an unusual strength; antisocial personality in adulthood, involvement in drug markets or sex work and concurrent use of other illicit drugs were not adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison periods may include use of other drugs; only alcohol and cannabis use disorders are adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Violence perpetration outside intimate relationships: Self-Report Delinquency Inventory with custom items (attacking with a weapon, hitting, attacking with intent to hurt seriously or kill, armed robbery, brawls, sexual coercion, animal cruelty; carrying a hidden weapon as a proxy). Victimisation: two items on physical or sexual assault from a life-events measure derived from the Feeling Bad Scale. Intimate-partner violence: 22 items from the Revised Conflict Tactics Scale, perpetration and victimisation separately, for people in a relationship of at least a month (pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established self-report instruments; no record or informant corroboration, as the authors note (p. 6).
outcomes.operationalization: At least one reported act in a period classified the person as a perpetrator or victim for that period (pp. 2–3).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across four outcomes, three model sets, the dose-response analysis, the ecstasy comparison and the interaction terms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; exposure and outcomes were reported in the same interview.

analysis.effect_sizes: Population-averaged odds ratios for any use in a period against none (Tables 1–2, p. 4). Violence perpetration: unadjusted 2.51 (95% CI 1.75–3.59), Model 1 2.42 (1.56–3.76), Model 2 1.60 (1.01–2.54). Victimisation: 2.93 (2.08–4.10), 2.64 (1.74–4.01), 1.57 (1.00–2.47). Intimate-partner violence perpetration: 2.11 (1.50–2.98), 1.87 (1.27–2.74), 1.55 (1.04–2.30). Intimate-partner violence victimisation: 1.53 (1.15–2.04), 1.43 (1.06–1.93), 1.09 (0.80–1.49). Sex by use interaction for victimisation b = 0.62 (SE 0.13), stronger in women (p. 4). Dose-response, heaviest frequency against never, adjusted for fixed confounders only (Table 3, p. 5): perpetration once or twice 1.13 (0.64–2.02), up to monthly 1.40 (0.81–2.42), at least weekly 4.84 (2.48–9.46); victimisation 1.87 (1.13–3.11), 1.89 (1.15–3.11), 3.62 (1.88–6.96); intimate-partner perpetration 1.75 (1.05–2.90), 1.89 (1.15–3.11), 2.44 (1.26–4.71); intimate-partner victimisation 1.12 (0.72–1.74), 1.45 (0.95–2.22), 2.28 (1.24–4.19). Population attributable fractions: perpetration 14.5% (0.8–23.0), victimisation 13.5% (2.6–20.6), intimate-partner perpetration 12.9% (1.2–18.7), intimate-partner victimisation 2.8% (0–8.0) (p. 5).
analysis.covariates: See comparison; the dose-response models use a reduced set of fixed confounders (family socioeconomic status, sex, child IQ, adolescent anxiety disorder, childhood physical and sexual abuse, deviant peers, attention problems; p. 5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Full Model 2 results, the ecstasy models and the confounder details are only in an online supplement (not read). The pairwise tests between frequency categories that the methods describe (p. 3) are not reported.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Only 51 people used at least weekly, and data sparseness prevented repeated-measures dose-response models (p. 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Periods with any self-reported methamphetamine or amphetamine use went with about 1.6 times the odds of self-reported violence perpetration and victimisation and of intimate-partner violence perpetration in the same period after full adjustment, with lower limits of 1.00–1.04; the association with intimate-partner victimisation was not clear (1.09, 0.80–1.49). Adjustment for concurrent mental-health, alcohol and cannabis disorders and life circumstances roughly halved the excess odds. Higher odds were concentrated in the 51 people who used at least weekly, in an analysis adjusted for fixed childhood and adolescent factors only and not period-matched.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes: "Methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for violence perpetration and victimisation" (p. 1). The discussion says methamphetamine plays a substantial role in violence where its use is common (p. 5), a reading that rests on attributable fractions, which assume a causal effect; and that the associations are not fully accounted for by antisocial personality and concurrent use of other substances (p. 5), although adult antisocial personality was not measured and only alcohol and cannabis use disorders were adjusted for. The abstract describes the dose-response as compared with people who used less often, but only comparisons with people who never used are reported (Table 3). Against this, the discussion states that the temporal order within periods was unknown, which limited causal inference, and that most people who used did not engage in or experience violence (p. 5).

timeline.event: Within-person analysis of an Australian treatment cohort (McKetin et al., 2014), described here as showing a strong dose-dependent association between days of use and high hostility (p. 1, p. 5); on the encyclopedia's reading list, not yet read
Meta-analysis (sharing authors with this paper): pooled adjusted odds ratio for violence with any amphetamine use 1.4 (0.8–2.4); this cohort was published later and is not in it
This study: first general-population longitudinal analysis, by the authors' account
Analysis of methamphetamine use and crime in Australian longitudinal data by an overlapping author group (McKetin, Boden, Foulds and others); not yet read

replication.where_it_stands: The adjusted associations are in the same direction as the within-person treatment-cohort finding and close to the meta-analysis's adjusted point estimate, but they come from one cohort, sit near no association after full adjustment, and share authors with both the meta-analysis and the later crime analysis, so agreement among these sources is partly agreement within one research group.

funding.funder: Health Research Council of New Zealand (Programme grant 16/600); the study was previously funded by the National Child Health Research Foundation, the Canterbury Medical Research Foundation and the New Zealand Lottery Grants Board (Acknowledgements, p. 6). The 'Role of funding source' statement reads 'None' (p. 6).
funding.affiliations_note: University of Otago (Christchurch and Wellington; Christchurch Health and Development Study) and Curtin University (p. 1). Two authors (Foulds, McKetin) are authors of the 2019 meta-analysis cited in the same claim. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated short-interval measurement (for example monthly or diary-based) of methamphetamine use, other drug use and violence within the same people in a general-population or high-risk cohort, with biological verification of use, records-based violence outcomes and adjustment for involvement in drug markets, so that use can be shown to precede violence within person; the authors themselves propose micro-longitudinal designs (p. 6).

domains.note: An unusually wide set of prospectively measured childhood and adolescent confounders, plus concurrent mental-health, alcohol and cannabis disorders. Not adjusted for: other illicit drug use, involvement in drug markets or sex work, adult antisocial traits. Use and violence are reported for the same three-to-five-year period, so violence or victimisation may precede use (reverse causation), as the authors acknowledge. Model 2 also adjusts for factors that may lie on the causal path (psychotic symptoms, depression), which would bias towards no association.

Self-report of use of 'methamphetamine, speed, P, ice, etc', without biological verification, so methamphetamine is not separated from amphetamine; coarse frequency categories reported retrospectively for periods of three to five years.
Unselected birth cohort; selection into the analysis through attrition is considered under missing data.
Treatment, arrest or imprisonment after use, which could change both use and opportunities for violence, are not considered; probably uncommon in this general-population sample.
19–24% of the cohort missing at each of the four waves; the handling of missing waves and any comparison of retained and lost participants are not reported.

Self-reported violence without corroboration, collected in the same interview as drug use; people more willing to disclose drug use may also disclose more violence, which would inflate the association. Repeated interviews with a long-trusted study team may reduce under-reporting, as the authors argue.
No pre-specified plan; several model sets with interaction terms, a dose-response analysis adjusted for a reduced covariate set, and key results (full Model 2, ecstasy models) only in a supplement.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No single domain is high, but concerns in six domains act in part in the same direction (reverse causation within periods, unadjusted other drug use, correlated self-report), and the fully adjusted estimates sit at the margin of no association (lower limits 1.00–1.04), so together they substantially lower confidence that the adjusted association is real. The study is stronger than the cross-sectional literature: an unselected cohort, prospective childhood confounders and repeated measures. It may be cited for an adjusted association in the same periods in a general-population cohort, and for higher odds with at least weekly use; not for a causal effect, not for methamphetamine as distinct from amphetamine, and not for the population attributable fractions as shares of violence caused by methamphetamine.

key_findings.finding: Birth cohort of 1,265 children (635 male, 630 female) born in Christchurch in 1977; interviewed at 21 (1,025), 25 (1,003), 30 (987) and 35 (962), 76–81% of the original cohort. Use of methamphetamine (asked as methamphetamine, speed, P or ice) since the last interview was coded as any or none in each of four periods.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1. Participants, 1st paragraph; 2.2. Methamphetamine use, age 18–35, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Any use was reported by 5.5% at 18–21, 22.4% at 21–25, 14.4% at 25–30 and 7.8% at 30–35. Over ages 18–35, 751 (71.9%) never used, 124 (11.9%) used at most once or twice, 118 (11.3%) used more often but at most monthly, and 51 (4.9%) used at least weekly in at least one period.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1. Methamphetamine use age 18–35, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: 293 of 1,044 people used at least once (28.1%, editors' calculation); the abstract gives 28% and the methods 28.2%.

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted population-averaged odds ratios for any use in a period against none: violence perpetration 2.51 (95% CI 1.75–3.59), victimisation 2.93 (2.08–4.10), intimate-partner violence perpetration 2.11 (1.50–2.98), intimate-partner violence victimisation 1.53 (1.15–2.04). Violence perpetration in the period with use: 19 of the people using at 18–21 (33.9%) against 67 not using (7.0%).

Adjusted for childhood and adolescent confounders (Model 1): perpetration 2.42 (1.56–3.76), victimisation 2.64 (1.74–4.01), intimate-partner perpetration 1.87 (1.27–2.74), intimate-partner victimisation 1.43 (1.06–1.93). Further adjusted for depression, anxiety, alcohol and cannabis use disorders, life stress, unemployment and psychotic symptoms in each period (Model 2): 1.60 (1.01–2.54), 1.57 (1.00–2.47), 1.55 (1.04–2.30) and 1.09 (0.80–1.49).
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › 3.3. Adjusted models…, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The association with victimisation was stronger in women than in men (sex by use interaction b = 0.62, SE 0.13); no other age or sex interaction was significant.

Dose-response (heaviest frequency at ages 18–35 against never; adjusted for fixed confounders only): violence perpetration 1.13 (0.64–2.02) for once or twice, 1.40 (0.81–2.42) for up to about monthly and 4.84 (2.48–9.46) for at least weekly use; victimisation 1.87 (1.13–3.11), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 3.62 (1.88–6.96); intimate-partner perpetration 1.75 (1.05–2.90), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 2.44 (1.26–4.71); intimate-partner victimisation 1.12 (0.72–1.74), 1.45 (0.95–2.22) and 2.28 (1.24–4.19).
key_findings.note: Not adjusted for the time-varying covariates of Model 2 (alcohol and cannabis use disorders, mental health); repeated-measures dose-response models were not possible because of sparse data (p. 3). The analysis relates the heaviest frequency reported in any period to violence at any time from 18 to 35 (Methods 2.7, 3rd paragraph, p. 3), so the heaviest use and the violence need not fall in the same period or in that order.

key_findings.finding: Ecstasy (MDMA) use, analysed the same way, showed no statistically significant association with any of the four outcomes after full adjustment (all p > 0.05; the authors call the evidence inconclusive); 38.5% of the cohort reported ecstasy use against 28.2% methamphetamine use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.8, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Results › 3.5. Comparison with ecstasy exposure, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Estimates only in the online supplement (not read).

key_findings.finding: Population attributable fractions for any use, with the relative risk calculated from the Model 2 population-averaged odds ratio: perpetration 14.5% (0.8–23.0), victimisation 13.5% (2.6–20.6), intimate-partner perpetration 12.9% (1.2–18.7), intimate-partner victimisation 2.8% (0–8.0).

The authors state that they could not be sure of the order of use and violence within each interview period, which limited causal inference; that use and violence were self-reported and not corroborated; and that most people who used did not engage in or experience violence.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives identical results, OR 1.89 (1.15–3.11), for victimisation and for intimate-partner violence perpetration in the up-to-monthly category.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly a copying error in one of the two cells (each interval is symmetric on the log scale, so neither cell is impossible as printed); both values should be confirmed with the authors before citation.

reporting_issues.issue: The models behind Table 2 include age by use and sex by use interaction terms (Table 2 note e), but the paper does not say how age and sex were coded, so the printed odds ratios may describe the reference sex and period rather than everyone; for victimisation the sex interaction was significant (b = 0.62, SE 0.13).
reporting_issues.consequence: The single victimisation odds ratio may not describe both men and women; how to read the main-effect odds ratios is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The row '% Pooled over ages 18–35' in Table 1 is not defined. For intimate-partner victimisation it matches the person-period percentage computed from the counts (11.2% and 18.2%, editors' calculation), but not for violence perpetration (4.5% and 11.3% against the printed 11.8% and 26.3%) or the other two outcomes.
reporting_issues.consequence: The row cannot be read as one consistent quantity and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The lowest frequency category is described as once or twice only in any age period (Methods 2.2, p. 2; Table 3, p. 5) but as never more than 1–2 times per year (Results 3.1, p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The boundary between the two lowest categories is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says Table 3 displays percentages of each outcome by frequency of use (p. 5), but Table 3 shows odds ratios only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The absolute frequency of violence by category of use is not reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The time-varying covariates are listed as cannabis use disorder in the methods and the Table 2 note but as cannabis dependence in the results text, and the results list omits psychotic symptoms, which the methods and the note include (pp. 3–4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the adjustment set of Model 2 is reported inconsistently.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'Role of funding source' statement reads 'None' (p. 6), while the acknowledgements name a Health Research Council programme grant (p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably means the funder had no role; the funding itself is as given in the acknowledgements.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 note a says the dose-response models are adjusted for fixed confounding factors (see Table 2 Model 1), while Methods 2.7 and Results 3.4 say that only the factors significant in Model 1 were used and list seven of them (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the note can be read as the full Model 1 set. The reduced set given in the text, which analysis.covariates records, is the better-supported reading.

disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on pp. 2, 3 and 5. Page and the places named in the issue corrected; content unchanged.
